newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FOCUS-Russian harvest seen more bountiful.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Russian harvest seen more bountiful.

text.p: Russia said on Friday it would have a bigger harvest and grain to export this year, signalling some recovery in its troubled agricultural sector.
Agriculture Minister Viktor Khlystun said the harvest was finally breaking out of a two-year cycle of disaster.
But Russia would also import grain, he said.
"We have a real chance to show our competitiveness," Khlystun told a news conference, adding that Russia's export potential was in rye, barley and sunflower seeds and also wheat.

Khlystun said Russia's grain harvest would recover to 77-79 million net tonnes this year from 1996's 69.3 million tonnes, which was the second poor showing in a row and one of the worst on record in three decades.
"We have hopes for a pretty high harvest -- it will be higher than last year's and -- this is very important -- we'll get more quality grain this year," he said.

The bigger haul meant Russia would be able to export four million tonnes of wheat used for bread-making and six million tonnes of fodder. Russia's total grain export potential in coming years would hold to those levels.
But he said regional imbalances meant private traders would import 3.5-4.0 million tonnes of grains this year.
These days, the Russian government no longer imports grain. Private commodities houses bring everything from wheat to frozen chickens into Russia, which now imports up to half of its food.
Khlystun said high imports had spurred domestic food producers to get their act together -- but he beat a protectionist drum by slamming the quality of imported food.
"The determined expansion of food importers has forced domestic producers, especially food processors, to look at products in a different way, in terms of quality, appearance and packaging," he said.
But he added, "We must say that the quality of imported food is lower than that of domestic food."
Imported vegetable oils represent 31 percent of the Russian market, sugar 69 percent and poultry 65 percent.
Khlystun spotted some signs of recovery in the livestock sector, whose shrinkage has depressed demand for feed grains.
"For the first time this decade we are seeing a positive trend in livestock," he said. "Maybe it's timid, not indicative, but 26 regions have more cattle than they did last year."

He said grain quality in some regions was much better this year. But trade sources say such optimism, meant to bolster the morale of farmers who are lagging in bringing in crops due to wet weather and late sowing, may be misplaced.
"Quality is a problem this year," said Andrei Sizov of the SovEcon Ltd consultancy.
But Khlystun said structural changes were in the works.
"For many years, we were ashamed to show our food at exhibitions," he said. "Now we see a small meat factory with 40 or 50 different product types, and the packaging is not bad."
